memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "And the Lord said, 'I will cause all my goodness to pass in front of you, and I will proclaim my name, the Lord, in your presence. I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.'" - Exod 33:19 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Moses asks to see glory. God answers with goodness, His name, and His mercy.

That is deeply revealing. When God shows us His glory, He does not primarily display raw power. He displays character. His goodness is His glory. His mercy is His splendour. The most magnificent thing about God is what He is like.

Then comes a statement that must be handled with care: "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy." Sincere Christians have read this differently for centuries, and we will not settle those debates here. What the verse itself insists on is simpler and undeniable: mercy is never owed. It cannot be demanded, earned, or claimed as a right. If it could, it would not be mercy.

That should not frighten us. It should humble us and then reassure us — because the God who reserves the right to show mercy has, in fact, shown it lavishly. He sent His Son. He commands the gospel to be preached to all nations. He says that whoever comes to Him will never be driven away (John 6:37).

You cannot demand mercy. But you can receive it. It is being offered right now.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. What do you imagine when you think of God's glory?
2. Do you treat God's mercy as something owed to you?
3. How does knowing mercy is free change how you come to God?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Merciful God, Your goodness is Your glory. I claim no right to Your mercy — I simply receive it in Christ. Amen.
